title: Rahula's verses
hook: the son who says he is doubly fortunate, son of the Buddha and heir to the teaching (Theragatha, Rahula)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhaddiya sat under a tree and kept sighing, ah, what bliss, sukha. Your line was ah what bliss. Did one simple thing give you that, even for a moment? Today, a son with two inheritances. Day eight hundred seven.

Give me my inheritance. A small boy says it, walking behind a monk. In the Vinaya's telling, the Buddha has come back to his father's city, and Rahula's mother sends their son after him to ask for what a father owes. The boy follows, telling the monk he likes the shade he casts. The Buddha doesn't hand him land or gold. He asks Sariputta to ordain the boy. Much later, Rahula sings about that inheritance himself, in the Theragatha. Today, his verses.
screen: `GIVE ME MY INHERITANCE.` → `NOT LAND, NOT GOLD.` → `THE BOY SINGS LATER.`

segments.voice: First, the name. They call me Rahula the fortunate, he says, and I'm fortunate both ways. Once because I'm the Buddha's son. Once because I've come to see the teaching clearly. One inheritance by birth, one by practice, and he names both plainly. Second, what the second one asked of him. He describes himself as he was: blinded by pleasures, caught in a net, wrapped in craving, bound by carelessness, like a fish in the mouth of a trap. Being the Buddha's son, in his own telling, didn't spare him any of that. The first inheritance came free. The second he had to take up. Third, what he found. The pleasures are thrown off, he says, Mara's bond is cut, craving is pulled out root and all. He has grown cool, quenched. Fourth, go back to the boy in the road. In the Vinaya, the Buddha reflects that the inheritance the boy asked for brings trouble with it, and chooses to give him another kind, the kind nobody receives by blood. And the text doesn't end on the gift. Rahula's grandfather, King Suddhodana, comes to the Buddha in pain. He has watched a son leave, and now a grandson. He asks that no child be ordained without the parents' consent, and the Buddha agrees and makes it a rule. So the second inheritance cost someone something, and the Vinaya keeps that grief on the page. When Rahula sings doubly fortunate, the story behind the song has already shown both sides of the gift.
screen: `FORTUNATE BOTH WAYS.` · `A FISH IN THE MOUTH OF A TRAP.` · `GROWN COOL, QUENCHED.` · `A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF, A NEW RULE.` · then, large: `DOUBLY FORTUNATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you inherited. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing that came to you by birth: a face, a language, a habit of the hands, a family story. Just name it, without judging it. Then bring to mind one thing you inherited by choosing it: a practice, a line from a teacher, a way of working you picked up and kept. Name that too. If you pray, you can give thanks for both in your own way. If not, simply hold them side by side, the given and the taken up. The bell holds the time.
Rahula's verses. The Buddha's son, in the Theragatha, calls himself fortunate twice: by birth, and by the teaching he took up. Today's word.
Your line: doubly fortunate. Today, pass on one thing you inherited, a recipe, a story, a skill, to someone younger or newer than you. Day eight hundred seven.

howItsDone: The Vinaya traces its rule of parents' consent before a child is ordained to Rahula's story and his grandfather's grief, and communities that keep the Vinaya keep that rule with it.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. your small son follows you down the road asking for his inheritance. what do you give him?
options: a share of the royal treasure.
nothing: you send him back to his mother.
a different inheritance: you have him ordained.
fork.reveal: in the Vinaya the Buddha decides the boy should have an inheritance that brings no trouble, and asks Sariputta to ordain him. then the grandfather's grief arrives, and a new rule with it.

original.note: Pali dayajja: an inheritance, the thing the boy asks his father for.

trapdoor: what you thought: he was the Buddha's son, so of course he was holy.
what it means: Rahula calls himself fortunate twice, by birth and by the teaching, and says the second came only after craving's trap was thrown off.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's inheritance story ends not with the gift but with a grandfather's grief and a new rule: no child ordained without the parents' consent.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.54 (Rahula's inheritance and Suddhodana's request)

notes: Confirm the paraphrase of Thag 4.8: 'Rahulabhadda', fortunate both ways (son of the Buddha, and having the eye for/seeing the Dhamma); blinded by sensual pleasures, covered by a net, covered by craving, bound by heedlessness, like a fish in the mouth of a trap; pleasures thrown off, Mara's bond cut, craving uprooted, cooled and quenched.

Index hook says 'heir to the teaching'; the verse's second fortune is usually rendered as seeing/having the eye of the Dhamma. The script uses 'come to see the teaching clearly' and keeps the inheritance theme through the Vinaya story.

Vinaya Mv 1.54: Rahula's mother (unnamed there) sends him; he follows saying the ascetic's shade is pleasant; the Buddha reflects that the paternal inheritance brings trouble and gives him the noble one; Sariputta ordains him; Suddhodana's grief and the parental-consent rule. Confirm each detail.
howItsDone: confirm that the parental-consent rule remains in current Theravada practice.
Original: दायज्ज (dayajja). Confirm it is the word the boy uses in Mv 1.54 and the stress.
Editor: softened the howItsDone and trapdoor claims that the consent rule 'still stands' in current practice to what the Vinaya itself says.
Audit: checked against Thag 4.8 and Mv 1.54; no change needed.
